Chapter Eight: Gratitude and the Practice of Vigilance
You know, over time, that initial rush of freedom can start to fade. The old fears and longing for escape slip away, replaced by the steady rhythm of daily life. And before you know it, those big feelings of gratitude—the kind that once took your breath away—become a little quieter. They don’t just happen; you’ve got to nurture them. Picture a mother raising her child in a safe home. She used to worry about survival, but now she finds herself stressing over things like report cards and playdates. Sometimes, she even forgets to notice the abundance around her. Sure, the memory of scarcity is still there, tucked away, but it doesn’t shape every decision anymore. One afternoon, her child complains about something small—a toy that’s broken, a playdate that’s been canceled. For a split second, she’s annoyed. But then, it hits her. She remembers her own childhood, how she didn’t even dare to dream about having these kinds of problems. That’s when she realizes, gratitude isn’t something that just happens on its own. It’s something you show, something you teach, and something you practice every single day. Most people don’t realize how easily comfort can turn into complacency. Freedoms that once felt like miracles? They start to blend into the background, almost invisible. The dangers that used to keep you on edge? They fade, too. But this mother—she gets it. She knows that keeping your freedom means you can’t let your guard down. So, she teaches her child to notice what they have, to ask questions, and to care about what’s happening outside their own little bubble. There are days she feels caught between two worlds—never quite belonging to either. But she’s also discovered something powerful: her story makes a difference. It gets people talking, thinking, and remembering what really matters. And she’s learned that gratitude isn’t just an emotion—it’s a practice. It’s a way of seeing the world that keeps freedom alive, every single day.
